### On our radar
As Trump gets his hands on Venezuela’s oil, Cuba’s regime fears for its future

The Trump administration announced that Venezuela will turn over between 30 and 50 million barrels of sanctioned oil that will be sold by the US “for the benefit of the American people and the Venezuelan people”.
How much revenue will go to Venezuela was not disclosed.

The announcement offers some clues to how the US plans to use its leverage over interim Venezuelan authorities to consolidate its control over the Latin American country after kidnapping President Nicolás Maduro.
How long will the US take the reins of the nation?
What are its specific plans?
Those remain largely unanswered questions.
In an interview with The New York Times, President Donald Trump said US oversight of Venezuela would last “much longer” than a year.
Meanwhile, the government of acting president Delcy Rodríguez said it would release “a significant number” of political prisoners – yielding to one key US demand.
Across the Caribbean Sea, Cubans worry they could be next.

Thanks in large part to US sanctions, the island was already in the grip of a severe humanitarian crisis, with its population struggling daily due to rising food prices, medicine shortages, and regular power cuts.

Now, with its key regional ally effectively under Washington’s control, and with the US trying to cut off its vital oil supplies, the pressure on Cuba’s communist regime is growing.**For more, read our latest article on the situation inside Venezuela in the wake of Maduro’s abduction****.**
**Protests (again) in Iran, but are they different this time?**

Authorities in Iran cut internet access and telephone lines across the country as anti-government protests – spurred by plummeting currency values and inflation surging past 40% – drew thousands onto the streets,spreading from Tehran’s Grand Bazaar on 28 December to several other major towns and cities.
The Islamic theocracy is no stranger to protests, but these ones come after a damaging 12-day conflict between Iran and Israel in June 2025 that featured some of the largest US strikes in decades.
So far, at least 45 people, including eight children, have been killed in the protests, according to a Norway-based tracking group.
Local media has reported that 950 police and 60 Basiji paramilitary forces have also been injured.
In a 9 January address on Iranian state TV, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei accused the protesters of acting on behalf of Trump and said the US president had hands “stained with Iranian blood”.
Trump threatened the Iranian government,saying, “If Iran fires and violently kills peaceful protesters, as is its custom, the United States will save them.
We are ready and prepared to act.” Khamenei responded by telling Trump to “focus on the problems of his own country”.
His rebuke was echoed by Trump’s domestic critics, who were quick to point out the irony of the US president criticising a foreign government for alleged use of force (see below).
Fatal ICE shooting sparks US protests
An immigration enforcement (ICE) agent’s fatal shooting of a 37-year-old woman in Minneapolis on 7 January has sparked days of street protests in cities across the United States.
President Trump has claimed the agent fired in self-defence at a driver who was “very disorderly, obstructing and resisting, who then violently, willfully, and viciously ran over the ICE Officer”.
Bystander videos show the woman’s car turning away from the officer at the time of the shooting, with no one being run over.
Thousands have taken to the streets in Minneapolis, New York, Chicago, and other cities to demand accountability for the killing and ICE’s withdrawal from their communities.
On 8 January, a US Border Patrol agent shot and injured two people in Portland, Oregon.

An official from the US Department of Homeland Security said the victims are suspected members of Tren de Aragua, the Venezuelan drug gang that Trump claims is waging war against the US under the orders of Maduro.
Rift between Saudi Arabia and UAE over Yemen deepens

The last month has witnessed a dramatic ramping up of tensions between forces in south Yemen backed by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, underlining what close observers of the country’s more than 10-year war already knew: The coalition fighting Houthi rebels is really an alliance in name only.

The Southern Transitional Council (STC), which is backed by the UAE and seeks independence for south Yemen, is a powerful part of the country’s internationally recognised government and Presidential Leadership Council (PLC).

In early December, the STC (itself composed of various militias)began taking territory in the oil-rich province of Hadramuht, angering Saudi Arabia, which backs other political forces and militias on the anti-Houthi side of the war.
Clashes and Saudi airstrikes then led the UAE to announce a withdrawal of its forces, with Saudi Arabia claiming it had taken back territory from the STC, including the capital, Aden.

Riyadh talks to de-escalate the crisis are now up in the air, with Saudi Arabia accusing the UAE of having spirited STC leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi out of Yemen by boat, and the STC alleging that members of its delegation to Riyadh have been detained as a rift (and possible disbanding) emerged within the separatist group.
While Saudi Arabia and the UAE have long been close allies, their policies over Yemen and the region have diverged.

Yemeni civilians – who have seen a decrease in ground fighting and airstrikes over the past few years (but no real peace) – can only wait and see what this latest phase of foreign meddling means for the war and for their lives.
Climate, gender targeted as US pulls out of international bodies
The United States has announced its withdrawal from 66 international organisations, including 31 UN entities.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised the organisations as “dominated by progressive ideology and detached from national interests”, as the exit list took aim at many groups working on gender or climate issues.

Among the most significant – though unsurprising – exits was from the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, though the US administration has not participated in this body’s work since President Trump took office and withdrew from the Paris Agreement.
Under Trump, the US has also had little to no interest in many other groups appearing on the list, like the UN Population Fund (UNFPA).
The withdrawal announcement represented the culmination of a US review into its multilateral memberships, which accompanied last year’s assault on the US aid budget and institutions.
While some mourned another blow to the multilateral system, other analysts said the move was “more bark than bite”.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres vowed the UN would “continue to carry out our mandates with determination”
Israel raises eyebrows with shock Somaliland recognition
Israel’s foreign minister visited Somaliland this week on the heels of his country’s surprise recognition of the breakaway territory in late December.
That move triggered international uproar.
Somalia condemned it as “unacceptable interference” in its affairs, and the Arab League and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation swiftly added their rebuke.

In becoming the first country to embrace Somaliland – which unilaterally declared independence more than 30 years ago – Israel snubbed the convention that the world follows the lead of the African Union.
So why did Israel do it?
A military base at the southern entrance to the Red Sea seems a likely dividend.
It’s a chokepoint for global maritime traffic, enabling Israel to flex as a regional hegemon with the backing of the United States.
It would serve as a threat to Houthi power in Yemen, and a possible check on rival Türkiye’s influence in Somalia.
There is another possibility: that Somaliland becomes the exile home for Palestinians expelled from Gaza.

### In case you missed it
**CAMBODIA/CHINA:** Cambodia handed over a billionaire businessman accused of running a massive crypto scam to Chinese officials.
Chen Zhi,a Chinese national, is accused of operating a multi-billion dollar crypto scheme that authorities said was built on online fraud and exploitation of trafficked workers.
The UN estimates that at least 100,000 people are forcibly held to work on online scams in Cambodia, and 120,000 in Myanmar.
**CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC:** President Faustin-Archange Touadéra secured a third term after an election boycotted by the main opposition coalition.
Touadéra was able to run again thanks to a 2023 constitutional referendum that scrapped presidential term limits, and he campaigned on improving security.
Russian mercenaries and Rwandan troops have helped him push back some rebel groups –but armed factions are still active, and pro-government military campaigns have come at a steep cost to civilians.
**DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO:**Fighting is continuing around Uvira in eastern DR Congo despite December’s US-brokered ceasefire and the withdrawal of Rwanda-backed M23 rebels from the city.
Kinshasa has accused the M23 of killing 1,500 civilians since December.
Meanwhile, nearly 90,000 refugees sheltering inside Burundi are facing shortages of food and water.
Burundi’s closure of the border has worsened their plight, while depriving Burundians of cross-border work opportunities.

**GREENLAND:** Top diplomats from Denmark and Greenland visited the White House on 8 January to address President Trump’s renewed push to either purchase or seize Greenland, having already told US lawmakers they had no plans to discuss ceding the Arctic territory.
Trump has said the vast island is vital for US security.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has said a US invasion of Greenland would mean the end of NATO.

**ISRAEL/PALESTINE:**A new report from the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) says Israel is violating international laws and conventions against racial segregation and apartheid in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.The report says Israel’s discrimination against Palestinians has worsened over the past three years, and its laws, policies, and practices have an “asphyxiating” impact on their daily life.
**LEBANON:** Lebanon’s army says it has taken over operational control of the south of the country, previously controlled by Hezbollah, the first phase of its plan to disarm non-state groups.
Israel, which continues to bomb what it says are Hezbollah targets on a regular basis despite a November 2024 ceasefire, said the efforts were encouraging but “far from sufficient”.
**SOMALIA:**A WFP spokesperson has told Reuters the UN agency has retrieved 75 metric tonnes of aid following the demolition of a warehouse in Mogadishu.
The US had earlier suspended assistance to the Somali government, accusing officials of forcibly demolishing the warehouse and seizing aid.
Somali authorities said the warehouse was located in a port area undergoing redevelopment and insisted the supplies were under WFP custody.

**SUDAN:**The war between the national army and the paramilitary-turned-rebel Rapid Support Forces – and the various armed groups supporting both sides – has now reached 1,000 days, with famine conditions spreading, and 11.5 million people displaced.
Abuses against civilians continue unabated with at least 13 people killed, including eight children, in a suspected RSF drone strike on the city of el-Obeid.

**SYRIA:** Initial estimates report 21 people have been killed and more than 100,000 people have fled their homes during days of fighting between the Syrian government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) in Aleppo.
On 9 January,Syria’s government announced a truce, but Kurdish fighters said they would not evacuate the neighbourhoods they control, leaving the status of the ceasefire in question.
**UGANDA:** Political violence is ratcheting up in Uganda once more ahead of elections on 15 January.
President Yoweri Museveni is seeking a seventh term in office, and the government is cracking down on his opponent Bobi Wine and his supporters.

Wine is forced to wear a flak jacket and helmet while campaigning.UN human rights chief Volker Türk has condemned reports of arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearance, and torture of members of the opposition.
